prompt: How do you turn on Roblox's Server Authority mode, which other settings does it force, and where should gameplay logic that the client predicts live? Say which clock that logic should use.

Core logic goes in functions bound with RunService:BindToSimulation(), in a ModuleScript that runs on both client and server. The client predicts ahead of the server and rolls back and resimulates when it mispredicts.

Use time(), which is synchronised, fixed-step and rewinds during resimulation, not tick()/os.clock()/os.time(). Instance:Destroy(), reparenting and UserInputService events are not allowed inside the bound simulation; use InputActions for input.

prompt: Since mid-2026, how are DataStore request limits and storage limits calculated for a Roblox experience? Give the write-request budget formula and say how UpdateAsync counts against the budgets.
answer_key: Request budgets are experience-wide: they scale with total CCU across all servers and, since 29 July 2026, are shared with Open Cloud requests. Per-server limits still exist and can be configured, for example with SetRateLimitForRequestType.

Per-minute formula is base + CCU x multiplier: write = 300 + 20 x CCU and read = 300 + 40 x CCU (list = 300 + 2 x CCU, remove = 300 + 40 x CCU). Full credit needs the correct write multiplier and base 300; a base of 250 earns partial credit (see README, disputed items).
Each UpdateAsync call uses one read and one write.
Storage limit = 500 MB + 1 MB x lifetime users, up from a 100 MB baseline. Only the latest version of each key counts toward it.

responses.R1: Limits are per experience (pooled across servers), per minute, scaled by concurrent users. Write budget = 300 + 20 x CCU per minute (some docs list 250 + 20 x CCU; design for the lower). Read = 300 + 40 x CCU, List = 300 + 2 x CCU, Remove = 300 + 40 x CCU. Storage = 500 MB + 1 MB x lifetime unique players (compressed). Per key ~4 MB/min write; request size rounded up to the next KB. UpdateAsync counts as one read AND one write against the budgets.
responses.R2: Since July 2026 the limits are per experience, and in-game and Open Cloud requests share one budget per minute. The budgets are: Read = 300 + 40 x CCU, Write = 300 + 20 x CCU, List = 300 + 2 x CCU, Remove = 300 + 40 x CCU. Per key, write throughput is 4 MB/min (read 25 MB/min). Storage is 500 MB + 1 MB per lifetime player. UpdateAsync counts as one read plus one write. The old per-server limits still exist but are no longer the binding constraint. A bulk Open Cloud job can starve live servers, so throttle it yourself.
responses.R3: Since July 2026 limits are per experience (shared by all servers and Open Cloud), scaling with concurrent users, measured per minute: Read 300 + 40 x CCU, Write 300 + 20 x CCU, List 300 + 2 x CCU, Remove 300 + 40 x CCU (some docs show a 250 base; design for the lower). Per server defaults still exist (e.g. write 60 + 40 x players). Per-key throughput: 4 MB/min write, 25 MB/min read, each request rounded up to the next KB. Storage is 500 MB + 1 MB per lifetime unique player (compressed). UpdateAsync counts as one read AND one write against the budgets. Overflow queues (30 per type) then errors 301-306.

Write budget = 300 + 20 x CCU per minute (the base was 250 before 2026-07-29). Read = 300 + 40 x CCU, List = 300 + 2 x CCU, Remove = 300 + 40 x CCU. Per key: 4 MB/min write and 25 MB/min read throughput, with each request rounded up to the next KB. Per-server request queues hold 30 requests. UpdateAsync consumes one Read plus one Write. Per key there is a 4 MB/min write throughput limit. Storage limit: 500 MB + 1 MB per lifetime player. prompt: My Roblox game sells loot crates for Gems. Gems can be bought with Robux, and there is also a 'Luck Potion' developer product that improves crate odds. What do Roblox's paid random item rules require me to show players, and what must I check for each player?
answer_key: The rules apply because Gems can be bought with Robux. Indirect purchases count too, including in-game currency bought with Robux, keys, re-roll tokens and spin tickets.

Before the player spends, show every possible outcome with its numerical odds as a percentage. The percentages must sum to exactly 100%; rounding is allowed if a disclaimer is shown. Long lists can sit behind a descriptively labelled pop-up, such as a 'Details' button, but not a bare (i) icon.
Luck Potion: explain its numerical effect before purchase, and update the displayed odds dynamically while it is active.

Per player, check PolicyService:GetPolicyInfoForPlayerAsync(). If ArePaidRandomItemsRestricted is true, block the purchase or use a permitted alternative (free earnable path, fixed disclosed order, sell items directly). If IsPaidItemTradingAllowed is false, don't let that player trade paid outcomes.

Before purchase you must show every possible outcome with its numeric odds (totals exactly 100%, rounded with disclaimer, no non-zero shown as 0%), reachable through a clearly labelled control. The Luck Potion must state its numeric effect before purchase, and while active the displayed odds must update to the player's actual boosted odds. Per player, on the server, call PolicyService:GetPolicyInfoForPlayerAsync and check ArePaidRandomItemsRestricted; if true (or the call fails/key missing - fail closed) don't let them buy/open paid crates (or the potion), offering a compliant alternative such as direct purchase. Enforce in the server purchase path, not just the UI.

Before purchase, show the odds of every possible item as numeric percentages that sum to 100%, behind a clearly labelled Info or Details button (a bare (i) icon isn't enough). The Luck Potion changes the odds, so you must explain numerically how it changes them before purchase, and the displayed odds must update while the boost is active. Per player, call PolicyService:GetPolicyInfoForPlayerAsync on the server. If ArePaidRandomItemsRestricted is true, don't sell random crates for paid currency: hide or block them, or offer a free or direct-purchase alternative. If IsPaidItemTradingAllowed is false, block trading of paid items. Fail closed: if the lookup fails, treat the player as restricted. Re-check on the server in the purchase and receipt handlers, not only in the UI.

Show, before purchase, every possible item with numeric odds summing to 100%, reachable from a clearly labelled Info/Details/Odds button near the purchase (not a bare icon). prompt: What are the correctness rules for a Roblox developer product ProcessReceipt callback? Explain why players sometimes get charged and receive nothing, or receive an item twice.
answer_key: Return Enum.ProductPurchaseDecision.PurchaseGranted only after the benefit has been granted and durably saved. Return NotProcessedYet on any failure, such as data not loaded, a failed save or the player not being in the server.

The callback can run again for the same purchase: on rejoin, on the next purchase, and even on two servers at once if the user joins another server before it returns. So it must be idempotent: record the PurchaseId and skip granting if that purchase was already handled.

Set ProcessReceipt only once, in a single server-side Script, and handle every product there. Using the newer MarketplaceService:BindReceiptHandler (which returns ReceiptDecision.Processed or NotProcessedYet) also earns full credit.
Never grant from PromptProductPurchaseFinished or any other client signal: it does not mean the purchase succeeded and can be spoofed.

responses.R1: Rules: (1) Assign MarketplaceService.ProcessReceipt exactly once (one handler routes all products). (2) Make it idempotent per receiptInfo.PurchaseId: record processed PurchaseIds (ideally in the same player profile as the grant) and if already processed return PurchaseGranted without granting again. (3) Grant and persist the item plus the PurchaseId together, and only after the save succeeds return Enum.ProductPurchaseDecision.PurchaseGranted. (4) On any failure/doubt (player not in server, data not loaded, DataStore error, unknown product) return NotProcessedYet so Roblox retries later (next join). (5) Never yield forever; never grant in PromptProductPurchaseFinished. Charged-but-nothing: returning PurchaseGranted even when the grant/save failed or the player left, so Roblox never retries. Double grants: no PurchaseId dedupe (Roblox re-calls the callback after a timeout/crash/server change, or on rejoin) or granting in both ProcessReceipt and PromptProductPurchaseFinished.
responses.R2:
ProcessReceipt correctness rules:
- Set exactly one ProcessReceipt callback, on the server.
- Make it idempotent per receiptInfo.PurchaseId. Record granted PurchaseIds in a DataStore (or in session-locked player data), and if an ID is already recorded, return PurchaseGranted without granting again.
- Return PurchaseGranted only after the grant has been durably saved.
- If the player is not in the server, the product is unknown, the data isn't loaded, or the save failed or threw, return NotProcessedYet. Roblox then retries later, for example when the player rejoins.
- Never yield forever, and wrap DataStore calls in pcall.

Charged but nothing received: the callback returned PurchaseGranted even though the save failed, or the player had left. It can also error or return nil and the grant is lost.
Item received twice: there was no PurchaseId check. Roblox retries any receipt that wasn't acknowledged, for example when the server crashed after granting but before returning, or when it returned NotProcessedYet after granting. Read-modify-write SetAsync races make this worse. Use UpdateAsync so the grant and the PurchaseId record are saved atomically.
responses.R3: Rules: (1) Assign ProcessReceipt exactly once, on the server. (2) Return PurchaseGranted only after the grant is durably saved. If the player is missing or anything fails, return NotProcessedYet, and Roblox will retry later or on rejoin. (3) Be idempotent by receiptInfo.PurchaseId: record processed PurchaseIds in the player's saved data, in the same UpdateAsync or atomic save as the grant, and if the ID is already recorded return PurchaseGranted without granting again. (4) Don't yield forever or error. pcall the DataStore calls and use UpdateAsync rather than Get-then-Set. (5) Look the product up by ProductId. Charged but nothing: the callback returned PurchaseGranted even though the save failed or the player had left, or it errored (for example, a nil player). Received twice: the callback granted, then failed before returning, or returned NotProcessedYet after granting, so Roblox retried and it granted again with no PurchaseId check. A race with a non-atomic Get+Set can also do it.
responses.R4: Rules: there is one ProcessReceipt for the whole game, set in one server script; if two scripts assign it, one never gets receipts. Grant the item and save it inside the callback. Return PurchaseGranted only after the grant has been durably saved. Otherwise return NotProcessedYet, for example when the player has left, the profile is not loaded or the save failed, and Roblox will retry. Make it idempotent: record each PurchaseId in the player's own data in the same atomic save (UpdateAsync or a session-locked profile) as the grant, and skip the grant if the PurchaseId was already processed. Don't yield forever and don't error out. Charged but nothing received: PurchaseGranted was returned before or despite a failed save, the grant happened outside the handler, or it went into an unloaded profile. prompt: When should you use UpdateAsync instead of SetAsync for Roblox player data, and what rules must the UpdateAsync transform function follow?
answer_key: SetAsync overwrites without looking at the current value, so two servers setting the same key at once can make data inconsistent. UpdateAsync reads the current value first, which makes it safer when several servers may write the same key.
The transform function can be called several times (it reruns if another server updated the key in between), so it must have no side effects outside its return value.
The transform function cannot yield: no task.wait() and no other yielding calls inside it.
Returning nil cancels the update. The function receives the current value and a DataStoreKeyInfo.

responses.R1: Use UpdateAsync whenever data could be written by more than one server/session or you read-modify-write (player data, counters, receipts, trades): it reads the current value and writes atomically with conflict retry, whereas GetAsync+SetAsync can overwrite newer data (rollbacks/dupes). SetAsync is only fine for blind overwrites of data nobody else writes. Transform rules: must not yield (no task.wait or other Async calls); may run multiple times, so no side effects and reset any flags on entry; return nil to cancel the write; return the new value; pass through userIds/metadata from keyInfo or they are wiped; check the session lock inside the transform.
responses.R2: Use UpdateAsync whenever the new value depends on the old one or several servers could write the same key (player data across teleports/rejoins, currency, purchase records, session locks); SetAsync blindly overwrites and can clobber a newer save. It also costs a read + write. Transform rules: it may be called multiple times (retries on conflict), so it must be pure: no yielding, no side effects (don't grant items, fire remotes or change state), deterministic from the old value; return the new value or nil to cancel the write; handle a nil old value (new player); don't mutate shared state outside; validate the session lock/version inside it and return nil if another server owns the data; keep it fast and within size limits.
responses.R3: Use UpdateAsync for any read-modify-write: incrementing, merging, session locks, and data other servers might touch. It is atomic, retries on conflict and sees the current value. SetAsync after GetAsync can overwrite newer data, which causes rollbacks and duplicated items. Use SetAsync only for blind overwrites (for example an admin restore while the player is offline). Transform rules: it gets (oldValue, keyInfo), and keyInfo is nil for a new key. Return the new value, or nil to cancel the write. It must not yield (no task.wait, other Async calls or remote invokes). It can run several times, so keep it pure and don't mutate captured live tables. Return userIds and metadata (keyInfo:GetUserIds()/GetMetadata()) or they get cleared. Check session-lock ownership inside it, and wrap the call in pcall.
responses.R4: Use UpdateAsync whenever the new value depends on the old one or multiple servers might write the key (player data, counters, receipts, trades): it reads the latest value and retries if another server wrote in between, avoiding clobbering; SetAsync blindly overwrites (fine only for write-once/independent values). Player data should also use a session lock. Transform rules: must not yield (no task.wait, no other Async/DataStore calls, no remote invokes); may run multiple times, so be pure/idempotent and reset any flags on entry - no side effects like granting items or firing remotes inside; return nil to cancel the write; return the new value (plus keyInfo:GetUserIds() and keyInfo:GetMetadata() if you want to keep them, otherwise they are cleared); handle a nil input (new key) explicitly; keep size under limits. Wrap the call in pcall.
responses.R5: Use UpdateAsync whenever the new value depends on the old value or more than one server could write the key, which covers player data, currency, receipts and session locks. SetAsync blindly overwrites, and a GetAsync followed by SetAsync can lose updates. Transform function rules: it receives (oldValue, keyInfo) and returns (newValue, userIds, metadata). Return keyInfo:GetUserIds() and GetMetadata() as well, or they get cleared. Return nil to cancel the write. It must not yield. It can run several times when there is contention, so keep it pure: no granting items, firing remotes or other side effects inside it, only compute from the input. Handle oldValue == nil for new players. Wrap the call in pcall with retry and backoff. UpdateAsync costs one read plus one write.
responses.R6: Use UpdateAsync whenever the new value depends on the old one (currency, inventory, counters), when several servers might write the same key (trading, teleports, rejoin), or for session locking and receipt deduping. It reads and writes atomically, so concurrent writes can't silently overwrite each other. SetAsync blindly overwrites. It's only acceptable for a fresh, independent value, and even then it risks clobbering newer data. Transform function rules: it must be fast and must not yield (no waits, no other DataStore calls, no remotes). It may be called multiple times, so it must be pure, with no side effects like granting items. Treat the old value as possibly nil and validate it. Return the new value, or return nil to cancel the write. Don't mutate shared state outside it. Keep the result under the 4 MB value limit. Remember that UpdateAsync costs a read plus a write, and pcall it.
responses.R7:
Use UpdateAsync whenever the new value depends on the old one, or when several servers could write the same key. Examples are currency changes, session locks, receipt records, and save-on-leave racing a teleport. SetAsync blindly overwrites, so a stale server can clobber newer data. Plain SetAsync is fine only for a first-time or unconditional write.

Rules for the transform function:
- It must not yield. No waits and no other DataStore calls.
- It may run several times on a conflict, so it must be pure and deterministic with no side effects such as granting items or firing remotes. Do those after the call succeeds.
- Return the new value, or return nil to cancel the write.
- Treat the old value as possibly nil (new player) or newer than you expected.
- Don't mutate shared tables you'll use outside it.
- Wrap the call in pcall with retry and backoff.

UpdateAsync costs 1 read + 1 write against the budgets.

prompt:
Is this server-side trade-offer validation safe? If not, why not, and how do you fix it?

```lua
offerRemote.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player, gold)
    if typeof(gold) ~= "number" then return end
    if gold < 0 or gold > player.Gold.Value then return end
    createOffer(player, gold)
end)
```
answer_key: It is not safe. NaN has type 'number' and every comparison with it is false, so a NaN offer passes both checks (+/-inf is also a problem).
Fix: reject non-finite numbers with math.isfinite(gold), or detect NaN with gold ~= gold, then check range (and integer if needed) against server-held state.
General rule: treat every remote argument except the automatic first Player argument as attacker-controlled.

Not safe. typeof(gold) == 'number' passes NaN and inf: NaN fails every comparison so `gold < 0` and `gold > Gold` are both false and NaN gets through; it also allows fractional values. Also the check is time-of-check only: gold isn't reserved, so a player can make many offers (or spend the gold) before trades settle, double-spending. Fix: reject non-finite and non-integer values and escrow at creation:
```lua
offerRemote.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player, gold)
	if typeof(gold) ~= "number" or gold ~= gold or gold % 1 ~= 0 then return end
	if gold <= 0 or gold > player.Gold.Value then return end
	if hasOpenOffer[player] or not rateOk(player) then return end
	player.Gold.Value -= gold -- escrow (refund on cancel)
	hasOpenOffer[player] = true
	createOffer(player, gold)
end)
```
(gold ~= gold catches NaN; gold % 1 ~= 0 catches fractions and inf.) Re-validate both sides again when the trade completes.

A NaN number passes typeof(gold) == 'number', and every comparison with NaN is false, so 'gold < 0 or gold > player.Gold.Value' never rejects it. createOffer then runs with NaN, which can corrupt balances or be used to dupe. prompt: A sword-swing animation and the default walk animation both animate the right arm. While walking, the swing looks weak or doesn't show. Explain how Roblox decides which animation wins on a limb, and how weights work.
answer_key: Priority order from lowest to highest: Core < Idle < Movement < Action < Action2 < Action3 < Action4. Core is the lowest even though its enum value is 1000.
On each limb, the highest-priority playing track wins. Set the swing to Action or higher, in the Animation Editor or through AnimationTrack.Priority.
Tracks with the same priority are blended by weight, set through AnimationTrack:Play(fadeTime, weight) or AdjustWeight (WeightTarget defaults to 1; weight 0 shows nothing).

responses.R1: Roblox resolves per joint by AnimationPriority (Core < Idle < Movement < Action < Action2 < Action3 < Action4). The highest-priority playing tracks that animate a joint claim weight first; only leftover weight (1 - their total) passes to lower priorities. The default walk is Movement priority; if your swing was authored/loaded as Core or Idle (or Movement and blending equally), walk wins or splits the arm, so the swing looks weak. Fix: set the swing track's Priority to Action (or higher), play it at weight 1 (AdjustWeight/Play(fade, weight)). Weight: within the same priority tracks blend proportionally by weight; a higher-priority track at weight 0.6 gives a 60/40 mix with the lower layer; at 1 it fully overrides that joint. Only joints with keyframes in the track are affected, so the legs still walk.
responses.R2: Roblox resolves per joint: the highest AnimationPriority track (Core < Idle < Movement < Action < Action2 < Action3 < Action4) that animates that joint wins outright; lower-priority tracks only affect joints the higher one doesn't key. Within the same priority, tracks are blended by weight (weights normalized, e.g. 1 and 0.6 give roughly 60/40). If the swing is at Core/Idle or the same Movement priority as walk, it is averaged with or overridden by walk, so it looks weak. A weight below 1 (or a fade in progress) with nothing beneath blends toward rest. Fix: set the swing track's Priority to Action (or higher) before Play, play at weight 1 (AdjustWeight) with a short fadeTime, and make sure the animation asset itself is saved with that priority.
responses.R3: Blending is per joint, and only tracks that key that joint compete. AnimationPriority decides it: Core < Idle < Movement < Action < Action2 < Action3 < Action4. Higher-priority tracks take weight first, and lower ones only get the leftover. If the swing is at Core or Movement (the default for many uploaded animations), it blends 50/50 with walk or loses. Set swingTrack.Priority = Enum.AnimationPriority.Action (before Play) or set it in the Animation Editor. Weights: within the same priority, tracks blend in proportion to weight (two at 1 = 50/50). A higher-priority track at weight 1 fully overrides lower ones on the joints it keys, and at 0.6 it leaves 40% to the lower ones. Use AdjustWeight and fade times. Also check the tool hold pose (toolnone), which keys the right arm.
responses.R4:
Roblox resolves animation conflicts per joint. A track only competes on the joints it actually keys.
- Higher AnimationPriority wins. The order is Core < Idle < Movement < Action < Action2 < Action3 < Action4.
- On each joint, the highest-priority playing tracks take weight first. Lower priorities get only the remaining weight, up to a total of 1.
- Tracks at the same priority blend in proportion to their weights.

Common causes of a weak swing:
- The swing was left at Core or Movement priority (the same as walk), so it gets averaged 50/50 with walk, or loses.
- It was played with a low weight. For example, with Action at weight 0.6, walk still gets the other 40%.
- The swing doesn't key the arm joints you expect.

Fix: set the animation's priority to Action (or higher) in the editor or with track.Priority = Enum.AnimationPriority.Action, and play it at full weight with track:Play(fadeTime, 1). AdjustWeight changes the weight at runtime. Weight is the target weight and fadeTime is the blend time. If the total weight on a joint is below 1 and nothing is underneath, the pose blends toward rest.
responses.R5: The Animator blends per joint, and a track only affects joints it actually keys. Higher AnimationPriority wins (Core < Idle < Movement < Action < Action2-4); higher-priority tracks take their weight first and lower priorities only get the leftover (1 - sum of higher weights). Within one priority, weights are summed; if the total exceeds the remaining weight they are normalised (two same-priority tracks at weight 1 split 50/50 - the weak swing). Fix: set the swing to Action (or higher), weight 1 via Play(fade, 1)/AdjustWeight, walk stays Movement. Then on the arm the swing fully wins; weight 0.6 would give a 60/40 mix. Weight < 1 with nothing beneath blends toward the rest pose.
responses.R6: Each joint is resolved separately by AnimationPriority: Core < Idle < Movement < Action < Action2 < Action3 < Action4. On any joint a track keys, the highest-priority playing track wins, and lower ones contribute only if the higher tracks' total weight is below 1. The default walk is Movement. If your swing is Core/Idle/Movement, it gets mixed with or overridden by the walk on the arm, so it looks weak. Set the swing's Priority to Action (or higher) before Play, in the animation editor or with track.Priority. Weights: tracks at the same priority blend by weight (two at weight 1 give 50/50). A high-priority track with weight 0.6 gives about a 60/40 mix with the layer below. Only joints the track actually keys compete, so an unkeyed arm keeps the walk. If the total weight is below 1 and nothing lies underneath, the joint drifts toward the rest pose. Fading weights (fadeTime, AdjustWeight) cross-blend the same way.

If its effective weight is below 1, the remainder goes to lower-priority tracks, so Action at 0.6 lets walk show 0.4. Tracks of equal priority blend by their relative weights: they're summed and normalised, and a total below 1 pulls toward the rest pose. Effective weight is the weight set by Play(fadeTime, weight) or AdjustWeight, multiplied by the fade-in progress. The swing looks weak because it's probably the same priority as walk (Movement or Core, often the default when authored), so the two average out. Or its weight or fade is low. prompt: My Blender model imports into Roblox Studio as an FBX about 100 times too big. Why, and what export settings does Roblox recommend?
answer_key: With default settings, Blender's FBX export often imports into Studio at an unexpectedly large scale (a unit-scale mismatch).
Recommended fix: in the FBX exporter, set Transform > Apply Scalings to 'FBX Unit Scale' and leave every other scale value at 1.0.

Alternatives: an export Transform Scale of 0.01, or a scene Unit Scale of 0.01. Caveats: re-imports into other tools may need scaling back up, working at 0.01 can cause Blender camera issues, and methods should not be stacked.
glTF/GLB export does not need these extra scaling settings.

responses.R1: It's a unit-scale mismatch. FBX is centimetre-based and Blender works in metres, so with unit scale 1 a 1 m object gets written as 100 FBX units (cm). Studio reads these as studs or rescales them, giving a 100x size. Recommended FBX export: Apply Scalings = 'FBX Unit Scale' (or FBX All), Scale 1.0, Forward -Z/Up Y (Forward Z, Up Y), Apply Unit on, Apply Transform/applied transforms (Ctrl+A in Blender), Add Leaf Bones off, Path Mode Copy + Embed Textures, Bake Animation off unless exporting clips. In the Studio importer, set the matching Scale Unit (Stud/Meter) and check the size. Use a single scaling method rather than scaling twice, and don't fix it by scaling in Studio for rigs, because animation translations stay in the old units.
responses.R2: Blender works in metres while Roblox works in studs, and the FBX unit-scale handshake gets multiplied twice. Blender's default FBX export writes Unit Scale 1.0 = 1 cm (Apply Scalings "All Local"/"FBX Units Scale" mismatch), and Studio's importer then converts cm to studs, so a 1 m object becomes about 100 studs. Recommended: Blender Scene Units = Metric with Unit Scale 1.0 (or 0.01 per some workflows), apply rotation and scale in Blender (Ctrl+A), and export FBX with Apply Scalings = "FBX Units Scale", Scale 1.0, Forward -Z / Up Y, and Apply Unit/Transform as recommended. In Studio's 3D Importer, check the file's scale units (set Scale Unit to Studs or match) and preview before importing. Or export glTF/GLB, which has no unit ambiguity. Don't fix it by rescaling in Studio, especially rigs.
responses.R3: Blender works in metres while Roblox uses studs; FBX stores unit scale (cm by default), so Blender's default unit scale/FBX scale method produces a factor of 100 (1 m exported as 100 cm units read as studs). Fix at source, not in Studio: in Blender keep Unit Scale 1.0 with 1 BU = 1 stud, apply scale/rotation (Ctrl+A) before export; in the FBX exporter use Path Mode Copy with Embed Textures on, Transform > Apply Scalings = FBX Unit Scale (or FBX All), Forward -Z / Up Y, Apply Unit on, Add Leaf Bones off, Bake Animation off unless exporting animation; and in the Studio 3D Importer check the scale/unit setting (Studs). GLB export avoids most unit issues.
responses.R4: It's a unit mismatch. Blender works in metres (1 unit = 1 m), and the FBX exporter's scale handling (unit scale or 'All Local' with a centimetre or 100x factor) gets read by Studio's importer as studs or centimetres, so the model ends up about 100x too big. Recommended: model at 1 Blender unit = 1 stud (check the size against a roughly 5-stud R15 avatar). In the FBX export use Apply Scalings: 'FBX Unit Scale' (or 'FBX All' with scale 1.0), apply all transforms first (Ctrl+A), Forward -Z / Up Y, and turn off Add Leaf Bones and animation simplify. In the importer, set the scale unit to Studs. Or export GLB, which avoids the FBX scale problem. Don't fix it by rescaling rigs in Studio.

Roblox recommends: set Blender Unit Scale to 0.01 (or keep metres and build at Roblox scale), and in FBX export use Apply Scalings = 'FBX Units Scale' (or 'FBX All'), Forward -Z / Up Y, Apply Transform/applied scale (Ctrl+A in Blender first), Add Leaf Bones off, Path Mode Copy with embedded textures. The size is a unit-chain mismatch. Blender works in meters with Unit Scale 1.0, but FBX stores centimeters. With the default "All Local" apply-scaling setting, the scale factor of 100 is baked in. prompt: I exported a .glb from Blender. In Roblox Studio my Mirror and Bevel modifiers are missing: only half the mesh is there and the edges are sharp. Why, and what is the catch with fixing it in the exporter?
answer_key: Blender's glTF exporter option 'Apply Modifiers' (export_apply) is off by default, so the base mesh is exported without the modifiers evaluated.
Enable Apply Modifiers (under Data > Mesh) to export the evaluated mesh. It applies all modifiers except Armature, so skinning still exports.

Catch: enabling Apply Modifiers prevents shape keys (morph targets) from being exported. Meshes that need shape keys must have those modifiers handled another way, for example applied manually beforehand.

responses.R1: glTF only stores mesh data. Live (unapplied) modifiers aren't in the file unless the exporter evaluates them, so you get the base mesh: half the model (no Mirror) and sharp edges (no Bevel). Fix: tick Apply Modifiers in the glTF exporter (Data > Mesh) or apply them manually. Catch: export-time Apply Modifiers bakes the whole stack, including ones you wanted live (e.g. the Armature modifier on rigs), and Blender's exporter can't apply modifiers on meshes with shape keys, which get dropped or block it. Custom normals may also change. For rigged meshes, apply Mirror and Bevel by hand on a copy and leave the exporter option off. Enable Clipping on Mirror so the seam doesn't split.
responses.R2: Modifiers are non-destructive and live only in Blender. The exporter writes the base mesh unless it evaluates the modifiers, so with "Apply Modifiers" unchecked you get the un-mirrored half and the un-bevelled sharp edges. Fix: tick Include > Apply Modifiers in the glTF exporter (Data > Mesh > Apply Modifiers), or apply the modifiers manually (Ctrl+A) on a copy before exporting. The catch: the glTF exporter can't apply modifiers on meshes that have shape keys, so the shape keys/morph targets are dropped or the modifiers are skipped. With an armature, Apply Modifiers would also bake the Armature modifier and break skinning. So for rigged or shape-keyed meshes, apply Mirror and Bevel manually first (before adding shape keys or skinning, or via an add-on), and leave the Armature modifier live. Also make sure Bevel uses enough segments and smooth shading, so you don't get only sharp edges.
responses.R3: Modifiers are non-destructive and live only in Blender. The glTF/GLB exporter writes the base mesh unless 'Apply Modifiers' is enabled, and it's off by default. So Mirror leaves half the mesh, and the Bevel geometry and smoothing are missing. The fix is to turn on Apply Modifiers in the exporter's Data/Mesh settings, or apply them manually before export. The catch: on a rigged or skinned mesh, Apply Modifiers also applies the Armature modifier and modifier stack ordering, which breaks the rig and skinning, or the export drops shape keys. For rigged meshes, manually apply Mirror and Bevel (above the Armature) and keep the Armature modifier live. Also apply transforms, limit to 4 bone influences, and check face normals and shading after Bevel.

Fix: enable Include > Data > Mesh > Apply Modifiers (with UVs and Normals) or apply the modifiers manually. Set Mirror with Clipping/Merge and order Bevel after Mirror.

Mirror and Bevel are non-destructive modifiers. Your .glb was exported with only the base cage, meaning modifiers weren't applied (the glTF exporter's Apply Modifiers option was off). That leaves half the mesh with no bevel geometry, so the edges are sharp.

Fix: enable Apply Modifiers in the glTF exporter, or apply the stack manually on a copy (top to bottom). For Mirror, use Clipping and put the origin on the symmetry plane. Then Merge by Distance and recalculate normals.

The catch: Apply Modifiers can't be combined with an armature or skinning. On a rigged mesh, applying modifiers drops or breaks the Armature modifier and skin weights, and shape keys are lost too. Only use it on static props. For rigged meshes, apply Mirror and Bevel manually before rigging, or on a duplicate, and keep only the Armature modifier live. Also, some Blender versions lose custom normals from Weighted Normal or Harden Normals during the conversion, so check the shading afterward.

If 'Apply Modifiers' is off in the glTF exporter, it exports the base mesh (the un-mirrored half, unbevelled). Fix: enable Include > Data > Mesh > Apply Modifiers (or apply them manually). Catch: Apply Modifiers in the exporter can conflict with rigs/shape keys: armature modifiers get baked into the rest mesh, and the glTF exporter skips shape keys (morph targets) on meshes with applied modifiers; also applied normals can change (weighted normals). So apply Mirror/Bevel manually on rigged/shape-keyed meshes, keep the Armature modifier unapplied, and check shading after export.
responses.R7: The glTF/GLB exporter writes the base mesh data unless 'Apply Modifiers' is enabled, so the Mirror (other half) and Bevel never get exported. Fix: enable Include/Data > Apply Modifiers (export_apply=True), or apply the modifiers manually before export. Catch: Apply Modifiers doesn't work with shape keys (Blender can't apply modifiers to a mesh with shape keys, so shape keys/morphs are lost or the modifiers skipped), and for skinned rigs it would also bake the Armature modifier/pose, so keep it off for rigs; applied bevels also raise triangle count. prompt: A Roblox HUD frame sized with UDim2.fromScale(0.3, 0.3) looks right on my monitor but stretched or squashed on other screens, and a button in the top-left corner is hidden by the notch or the Roblox top bar on phones. Explain both problems and give the fixes.
answer_key: Scale is relative to the parent's width and height separately, so the frame's shape follows the screen's aspect ratio. Fix: add a UIAspectRatioConstraint (AspectRatio = width/height); it enforces the ratio even on Scale-sized objects.

Fix the hidden button with ScreenGui.ScreenInsets = CoreUISafeInsets (the default when IgnoreGuiInset is false), which avoids both device cutouts and Roblox core UI such as the top bar. DeviceSafeInsets only avoids cutouts (IgnoreGuiInset = true switches to it). None is only for non-interactive backgrounds.

responses.R1: Problem 1: fromScale(0.3,0.3) is 30% of width and 30% of height independently, so on screens with different aspect ratios the frame's shape changes. Fix: add a UIAspectRatioConstraint (e.g. AspectRatio 1, DominantAxis), optionally UISizeConstraint/UIScale for min/max sizes; scale for position. Problem 2: the button sits where the notch/cutout and the Roblox top bar draw. Fix: keep interactive UI in a ScreenGui with ScreenInsets = CoreUISafeInsets (default; avoids top bar and notch) and SafeAreaCompatibility = None, offset using GuiService.TopbarInset if aligning beside the top bar; don't set ScreenInsets = None / IgnoreGuiInset on interactive HUDs. Put full-bleed decoration in a separate ScreenGui with ScreenInsets = None.
responses.R2: Stretching: UDim2.fromScale(0.3,0.3) is 30% of width and 30% of height, so on screens with a different aspect ratio the frame's shape changes. Fix: add a UIAspectRatioConstraint (e.g. AspectRatio 1) or size with Offset plus a UIScale computed from the viewport, and UISizeConstraint for min/max. prompt: Outline, in pseudocode or short Luau, a session-locked Roblox player-data system that prevents item duplication when players teleport or rejoin quickly.
answer_key: Load and lock atomically in one UpdateAsync: write a lock (server or job id / GUID, plus a timestamp) into the data or the key's metadata. If another server holds a lock that hasn't expired, don't proceed; retry or wait.
The lock expires. Refresh it regularly, for example in the autosave loop (Roblox's sample uses 180 s), so another server can take over a crashed server's lock once it expires.
Every read and write goes through UpdateAsync and checks that this server still owns the lock. The final save on PlayerRemoving writes the data and releases the lock in the same call.
game:BindToClose saves all remaining players in parallel, within the 30-second shutdown window.

      d = d or newDoc()
      if d.lock and d.lock.jobId ~= game.JobId and os.time() - d.lock.t < LEASE then
        return nil               -- locked by another server: cancel write
      end
      d.lock = {jobId = game.JobId, t = os.time()}
      return d

    d.lock = (not release) and {jobId = game.JobId, t = os.time()} or nil

prompt: Debug this. I set MeshPart.RenderFidelity = Precise on my hero meshes, but in my published game they still drop to lower detail at a distance, and changing the property seems to do nothing. What is going on?
answer_key: Workspace.MeshStreamingAndImprovedLoDs (mesh streaming with improved cloud LoDs, opt-in since April 2026) is Enabled. In that mode RenderFidelity is ignored on every MeshPart and meshes go through the new transcoder instead.

RenderFidelity is planned for removal in a later phase (Default is planned to map to Enabled). To compare, toggle the Workspace property (Studio asks for a restart), test in Studio, and report broken meshes with asset IDs.

responses.R1: RenderFidelity is not a runtime-scriptable property. It's baked when the MeshPart is created or imported (set it in Studio, via plugins, or in CreateMeshPartAsync options), so setting it from a game script has no effect. Also check that you actually saved and published the Studio edit. Precise does keep the mesh at full detail at any distance. Other things lower detail in a live game: (1) Model streaming LOD. With StreamingEnabled and the parent Model's LevelOfDetail = StreamingMesh (or Automatic), distant or unstreamed models are drawn as low-poly imposter meshes regardless of RenderFidelity. Set Model.LevelOfDetail = Disabled (and/or ModelStreamingMode = Persistent) for hero models. (2) Client graphics quality. Low quality levels and mobile devices reduce draw distance and detail, which Studio (often at max quality) doesn't show. (3) Automatic fidelity on other parts, such as unions, accessories and textures (Automatic steps down at about 250 and 500 studs). Verify with a test place on the target device.
responses.R2:
Your game almost certainly has Workspace.MeshStreamingAndImprovedLoDs set to Enabled (the newer default). In that mode every MeshPart uses mesh streaming with cloud-generated LoDs, and RenderFidelity is ignored. The property is also planned for removal. So setting it to Precise does nothing, and detail still drops at a distance.

What to do:
- Check that Workspace property first.
- To control quality, budget triangles at the source and author clean meshes.
- Keep important hero meshes reasonably dense, since LoD falls back based on distance and screen size.
- Don't rely on RenderFidelity.
- If you turn the Workspace setting off, RenderFidelity applies again (Automatic, Precise or Performance), but you lose streaming and improved LoDs.

Test in the published client, not just in Studio.
responses.R3: Your game almost certainly has Workspace.MeshStreamingAndImprovedLoDs enabled (mesh streaming / cloud-generated LODs). In that mode Roblox generates and streams LODs itself and MeshPart.RenderFidelity is ignored (the property is slated for removal), so Precise does nothing and meshes still drop detail with distance. Options: accept the automatic LODs (they also save memory), check/adjust the Workspace setting, reduce reliance on distance detail by budgeting triangles at the source, or author your own LOD meshes and swap them. RenderFidelity only applies when that system is off.
responses.R4: RenderFidelity isn't a normal runtime property: it can only be set in Studio/by plugins before publishing (scripts can't change it at runtime, and setting it in Studio may require re-upload/geometry processing), so script changes do nothing. More importantly, Precise only requests full detail; the client still lowers detail based on the player's graphics quality level, memory pressure and Roblox's streaming/LOD systems (model streaming LOD, mesh LOD on low-end devices), so on lower settings or mobile meshes still drop detail at distance. Studio typically runs at high quality so you don't see it there. Check: the property is actually set on the published MeshParts (not on a different copy), test with low graphics quality, and use ModelStreamingMode = Persistent / Atomic for key models; reduce mesh triangle counts so the low LOD looks acceptable. Note: in my lookup the vault had no note explaining this exact symptom; this is general knowledge.

Keep important meshes within a sensible triangle budget at the source, so the generated LoDs look fine. Don't put Precise on everything: Automatic is the recommended default, and Precise everywhere hurts performance.
